title: The encircling prayer
hook: Celtic Christians drew a circle around themselves with a finger, praying for protection

segments.voice: Yesterday, take, Lord, receive: the Suscipe, and the end of our time with Ignatius. Your line was your love and grace are enough. When you wanted more of something, did the line catch you? Day one thousand one hundred forty-nine.

A finger, pointed out at arm's length. A person turns slowly in place, sunwise, tracing a circle in the air all the way around. Then they step forward, and tradition says the circle goes with them. That's a picture from the Gaelic Christian world of the Scottish Highlands and islands. It begins a new stretch of this year's path: the Celtic way of prayer. Prayer close to the ground, to weather, to doors and roads and hearths. Today's word: caim. The encircling prayer.

Caim is a Gaelic word, given in English as a circle or an encompassing. The prayers that go with it ask God to surround a person: before and behind, above and below, on the right hand and the left. Some were said for oneself, some over a child, a traveler, a house. And notice what the circle is. It isn't a magic boundary. In the prayers, the circle is God. The person isn't building a wall; they're naming what's already around them. The Psalms already have the same picture. Psalm one hundred twenty-five, in the King James: "As the mountains are round about Jerusalem, so the LORD is round about his people." The city sits in its hills, and the hills become a picture of God on every side. Psalm one hundred thirty-nine says it more closely still: "Thou hast beset me behind and before, and laid thine hand upon me." Beset, hemmed in, but by care. The caim has a cousin some will know: the old Irish prayer called Saint Patrick's Breastplate, which tradition gives to Patrick. One stretch of it names Christ with me, before me, behind me, in me, beneath me, above me. Same shape: a person at the center, and Christ named in every direction. Why a finger? Because a gesture can carry a prayer when words won't come. It can be made in a hospital corridor, at a bus stop, beside a crib, without anyone hearing a word. And the prayers don't promise that nothing hard will happen. They name who is in the circle when it does.
screen: `THE CIRCLE IS GOD, NOT A WALL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: draw a circle and pray. If there's room, sit tall and stretch out your right hand, one finger pointing. Turn slowly, or just sweep your arm around you, tracing a circle. Then rest your hand in your lap. Name what's inside the circle with you: someone you love, a worry, the room itself. If you pray, you can say the line from Psalm one hundred thirty-nine: thou hast beset me behind and before. If not, just sit inside the shape you drew. The bell holds the time.
Caim. A Gaelic word for an encircling: a gesture and a prayer that name God on every side of a person.
Your line: circled by god. Today, trace a small circle with one finger before you walk into somewhere hard. Day one thousand one hundred forty-nine.

howItsDone: In the Gaelic tradition recorded in the Scottish Highlands and islands, a person in danger would trace a circle around themselves with a finger while praying for God's protection; some Christians today use caim prayers in personal and community prayer.

myth: in the caim prayers, the circle is a magic wall
in the prayers the circle is God, named on every side, not a wall the person builds.
Psalm 125 pictures the LORD round about his people like mountains
"as the mountains are round about Jerusalem, so the LORD is round about his people."
the caim promises nothing hard will happen
the prayers name who is in the circle when hard things come; they don't promise they won't.

fork.setup: you're about to walk into a hard conversation, and you remember the old Gaelic prayer. what does the caim do?
options: trace a circle and name God around you.
build a wall to keep everyone out.
fork.reveal: the caim names God on every side. it's a gesture you can make anywhere, without anyone hearing a word.

trapdoor: what you thought: drawing a circle for protection sounds like a spell.
what it means: a Gaelic Christian prayer naming God before, behind, above and below, with a finger tracing the circle.
what a scholar hears: the Psalms already have the shape: the LORD round about his people, as the mountains are round about Jerusalem.

notes: Caim: Scottish Gaelic, commonly glossed 'circle', 'encompassing' or 'sanctuary'. The gloss is a standard dictionary sense rather than a root claim; confirm.

The gesture (right forefinger extended, turning sunwise, the circle moving with the person) is from Carmichael's notes in Carmina Gadelica; framed as 'tradition says'. Confirm detail, especially 'sunwise'.
St. Patrick's Breastplate: attribution to Patrick is traditional; the 'Christ with me, Christ before me' stanza is paraphrased, not quoted. Confirm.
The hook places the caim in the Gaelic Christian world of the Scottish Highlands and islands (where Carmichael collected); the index says 'Celtic Christians'. Confirm.
First day of the Celtic way (Block B).
